_general.summary: Backend interviews test HTTP semantics, data integrity, authn/z, and operational failure modes under load.
_general.problem: Surface-level framework trivia without invariants (idempotency, timeouts, authz) fails real production scenarios.
_general.mechanics: State the invariant, describe the request path, name failure modes, and say how you detect/alert them.
_general.tradeoffs: Prefer simple designs with clear ownership over distributed complexity you cannot operate.
_general.troubleshoot: Ask for symptoms, SLOs, and recent changes before proposing rewrites.
_general.integration: 1) Clarify invariants. 2) Implement smallest correct path. 3) Add tests/metrics. 4) Document runbooks. 5) Load-test critical flows.

API integration test.summary: API integration tests exercise HTTP handlers against real-ish dependencies (DB/testcontainers) to verify contracts end-to-end.
API integration test.problem: Unit-only suites miss wiring bugs in pipes, auth guards, and migrations.
API integration test.mechanics: Boot Nest/Express app, seed data, call HTTP, assert response and side effects, reset DB between tests.
API integration test.tradeoffs: Slower than unit tests but higher confidence; keep a focused suite, not full prod clones.
API integration test.troubleshoot: On flake, isolate shared DB state and time dependence.
API integration test.integration: 1) Add testcontainers/DB. 2) Write critical-path API tests. 3) Run on PR. 4) Keep unit tests for pure logic.

API versioning.summary: API versioning evolves contracts without silently breaking existing clients—via URL, headers, or media types.
API versioning.problem: Breaking field meanings in place strand old mobile apps that cannot force-upgrade instantly.
API versioning.mechanics: Prefer additive changes; when breaking, introduce v2, dual-run, migrate clients, then sunset with metrics.
API versioning.tradeoffs: URL versions are obvious but noisy; header versions are clean but harder to explore. Avoid infinite parallel versions.
API versioning.troubleshoot: If clients break, check which fields changed meaning and whether you shipped a silent break.
API versioning.integration: 1) Publish compatibility policy. 2) Version only on breaks. 3) Dual-write/read as needed. 4) Track version usage. 5) Sunset with notice.

at-least-once delivery.summary: At-least-once delivery means consumers may see duplicates after retries; handlers must be idempotent.
at-least-once delivery.problem: Assuming exactly-once without a dedupe store double-charges or double-emails.
at-least-once delivery.mechanics: Acknowledge only after durable side effects, store processed keys, and send poison messages to DLQ.
at-least-once delivery.tradeoffs: Exactly-once is rare/expensive; usually at-least-once + idempotency is the practical design.
at-least-once delivery.troubleshoot: If duplicates appear, add idempotency table unique constraints.
at-least-once delivery.example: INSERT INTO processed_events(id) VALUES($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; -- skip if not inserted
at-least-once delivery.integration: 1) Make handlers idempotent. 2) Persist dedupe keys. 3) DLQ. 4) Metric retries/dupes.

backpressure.summary: Backpressure signals producers to slow down when consumers/queues cannot keep up, preventing unbounded memory growth.
backpressure.problem: Unbounded buffers under load OOM the process while appearing 'fine' until collapse.
backpressure.mechanics: Set max queue sizes, use stream backpressure, return 429/503 when overloaded, and autoscale on lag.
backpressure.tradeoffs: Dropping/shedding hurts UX but saves the system; buffering hides problems until failure.
backpressure.troubleshoot: Watch queue depth and RSS; if both climb, apply limits.
backpressure.integration: 1) Define limits. 2) Shed load. 3) Alert on depth. 4) Load-test. 5) Document degraded modes.

Buffer.summary: Buffer is Node's fixed-size binary memory type for bytes from sockets, files, and crypto.
Buffer.problem: Treating binary as UTF-8 strings corrupts data; unsafe Buffer alloc can leak memory contents.
Buffer.mechanics: Use Buffer.from/alloc for binary, set encodings explicitly, prefer Uint8Array APIs when portable.
Buffer.tradeoffs: Buffers are fast but easy to misuse with encodings; streams often beat giant buffers for large payloads.
Buffer.troubleshoot: If you see replacement characters, you decoded with the wrong encoding.
Buffer.integration: 1) Ban allocUnsafe without overwrite. 2) Explicit encodings. 3) Stream large payloads. 4) Add binary fixtures in tests.

cache invalidation.summary: Cache invalidation removes or updates stale entries so readers see fresh data after writes.
cache invalidation.problem: TTL-only caches serve stale critical data; manual deletes miss keys and leave ghosts.
cache invalidation.mechanics: Choose strategy per data: short TTL, explicit delete on write, or versioned keys after mutations.
cache invalidation.tradeoffs: Invalidation complexity is famous; sometimes prefer short TTL over perfect coherence.
cache invalidation.troubleshoot: If stale after write, log keys written vs invalidated and check race windows.
cache invalidation.integration: 1) Classify data freshness needs. 2) Invalidate on write paths. 3) Version keys. 4) Monitor stale incidents.

cache-aside.summary: Cache-aside (lazy loading) has the app read cache, on miss load DB then populate cache; writes update DB then invalidate cache.
cache-aside.problem: Write-through everywhere can slow writes; never caching thrashes DB.
cache-aside.mechanics: Implement getOrLoad with single-flight, set TTL, and delete/update cache after successful writes.
cache-aside.tradeoffs: Simple and common; stampeding herd on expiry needs locking or probabilistic early expire.
cache-aside.troubleshoot: If DB spikes at TTL boundaries, add stampede protection.
cache-aside.example:
let v = await redis.get(key);
if (!v) { v = await db.load(); await redis.set(key, v, 'EX', 60); }
cache-aside.integration: 1) Wrap reads. 2) Invalidate writes. 3) Stampede guard. 4) Metrics hit ratio.

chat backend.summary: Chat backends manage rooms, membership, message persistence, fanout, and presence with ordering guarantees.
chat backend.problem: Naive broadcast without persistence loses history; missing authz leaks private rooms.
chat backend.mechanics: Persist first (or reliably enqueue), fanout via pub/sub, authorize membership, and paginate history by cursor.
chat backend.tradeoffs: Fanout-on-write scales differently than fanout-on-read; choose by room size distribution.
chat backend.troubleshoot: If messages reorder, include monotonic server timestamps/ids and sort on client.
chat backend.integration: 1) Schema messages. 2) Authz rooms. 3) Pub/sub fanout. 4) History API. 5) Rate-limit sends.

circuit breaker.summary: Circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency temporarily, failing fast and allowing recovery.
circuit breaker.problem: Retry storms against a down dependency amplify outages.
circuit breaker.mechanics: Trip open after error rate/latency thresholds, short-circuit calls, probe in half-open, and serve fallbacks.
circuit breaker.tradeoffs: Breakers protect systems but hide dependency issues if alerts missing; tune thresholds carefully.
circuit breaker.troubleshoot: If breaker flaps, raise windows or fix timeouts that are too aggressive.
circuit breaker.example: // pseudo: if failures/total > 50% in 30s → open for 20s
circuit breaker.integration: 1) Wrap critical clients. 2) Set thresholds. 3) Fallback behavior. 4) Alert on open. 5) Test chaos.

connection pool.summary: Connection pools reuse DB/TCP connections to avoid handshake overhead and limit concurrent connections.
connection pool.problem: Unbounded connections exhaust Postgres max_connections under traffic spikes.
connection pool.mechanics: Size pools per instance relative to DB limits, fail fast on checkout timeout, and prefer transaction pooling for many tenants.
connection pool.tradeoffs: Larger pools increase throughput until DB CPU/locks contend; measure.
connection pool.troubleshoot: If 'too many connections', reduce app pools or add pgbouncer.
connection pool.integration: 1) Calculate budgets. 2) Cap pools. 3) Add timeouts. 4) Monitor wait time. 5) Consider pgbouncer.

contract testing.summary: Contract tests verify producer/consumer API expectations (schemas, status codes) without full E2E environments.
contract testing.problem: Frontend/backend drift breaks production when only manual QA exists.
contract testing.mechanics: Publish contracts, validate both sides in CI, and break builds on incompatible changes.
contract testing.tradeoffs: Contracts catch interface bugs early but not full business logic—still need some E2E.
contract testing.troubleshoot: If false positives, version contracts and allow additive changes.
contract testing.example: // CI: oasdiff / openapi-diff against main; fail on breaking
contract testing.integration: 1) Choose contract format. 2) Generate/validate in CI. 3) Version breaks. 4) Notify consumers.

controller.summary: Controllers adapt HTTP to application commands: parse input, call services, map results to status codes.
controller.problem: Fat controllers with business logic become untestable and duplicated across transports.
controller.mechanics: Validate DTOs, authorize, call services, return DTOs—no SQL in controllers.
controller.tradeoffs: Very thin vs useful orchestration: keep orchestration minimal and explicit.
controller.troubleshoot: If hard to unit test, logic is in the controller—extract services.
controller.integration: 1) Thin controllers. 2) Move logic to services. 3) Shared DTO validation. 4) Controller integration tests only for wiring.

correlation ID.summary: Correlation IDs propagate a request identifier across services/logs so you can reconstruct a single transaction's path.
correlation ID.problem: Disconnected logs make multi-service incidents nearly impossible to triage.
correlation ID.mechanics: Create/accept X-Request-Id, store in async local storage, inject into outbound calls and structured logs.
correlation ID.tradeoffs: IDs alone aren't distributed tracing spans, but they are a minimal must-have.
correlation ID.troubleshoot: If IDs change mid-flight, a client is overwriting—preserve inbound IDs when present.
correlation ID.example:
const id = req.headers['x-request-id'] ?? crypto.randomUUID();
logger.info({ requestId: id }, 'handling');
correlation ID.integration: 1) Middleware generate/propagate. 2) ALS storage. 3) Outbound inject. 4) Log field standard. 5) Dashboards by id.

CPU-bound workload.summary: CPU-bound work saturates the Node event loop when run on the main thread, delaying all requests.
CPU-bound workload.problem: Heavy JSON parse/crypto/image work in request handlers creates latency spikes under concurrency.
CPU-bound workload.mechanics: Measure loop lag, move CPU to worker_threads/native addons/queues, and set timeouts/backpressure.
CPU-bound workload.tradeoffs: Workers add complexity; for rare heavy jobs prefer async queues over in-request compute.
CPU-bound workload.troubleshoot: If p99 latency rises with CPU, check event-loop delay metrics and profiles.
CPU-bound workload.example:
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';
const w = new Worker(new URL('./heavy.js', import.meta.url));
CPU-bound workload.integration: 1) Profile. 2) Move hot CPU off-loop. 3) Queue long jobs. 4) Alert on loop delay.

DDD bounded context.summary: A bounded context is a linguistic and model boundary in DDD where terms have a specific meaning and a dedicated model.
DDD bounded context.problem: One enterprise-wide User model conflates meanings and creates brittle coupling across domains.
DDD bounded context.mechanics: Split models by language/team ownership, translate at edges, and keep transactions within a context when possible.
DDD bounded context.tradeoffs: Too many contexts create distributed complexity; too few recreate the ball of mud.
DDD bounded context.troubleshoot: If teams argue over field meanings, you've crossed a context without a map.
DDD bounded context.example: // orders.CustomerId vs crm.AccountId — different models, mapped at ACL
DDD bounded context.integration: 1) Name contexts. 2) Draw context map. 3) Split schemas/modules. 4) Add ACLs. 5) Align teams to boundaries.

distributed lock.summary: Distributed locks coordinate mutual exclusion across processes using Redis/etcd with TTLs and safe ownership tokens.
distributed lock.problem: Locks without TTL deadlock after crashes; non-token unlocks delete someone else's lock.
distributed lock.mechanics: Acquire with NX+TTL+token, extend if needed, unlock only with token compare, and design for lock loss.
distributed lock.tradeoffs: Locks are hard to get perfectly correct; prefer DB uniqueness constraints when possible.
distributed lock.troubleshoot: If two holders run, TTLs expired—shorten critical sections or use fencing.
distributed lock.example:
SET lock:job:1 token NX EX 30
-- unlock via Lua compare-and-del token
distributed lock.integration: 1) Prefer DB constraints. 2) If Redis lock, token+TTL. 3) Keep critical section tiny. 4) Chaos-test expiry.

distributed tracing.summary: Distributed tracing records spans across services (OpenTelemetry) to visualize latency and errors in a request graph.
distributed tracing.problem: Metrics alone cannot show which downstream hop caused a slow request.
distributed tracing.mechanics: Instrument frameworks, propagate context, export to a backend, and sample appropriately.
distributed tracing.tradeoffs: High sampling costs money; too low misses rare bugs. Tail-based sampling helps.
distributed tracing.troubleshoot: If traces broken, check header propagation and clock skew.
distributed tracing.example: // OTel Node auto-instrument Nest/HTTP and export OTLP
distributed tracing.integration: 1) Add OTel SDK. 2) Propagate headers. 3) Sample. 4) Link logs via trace_id. 5) Create service maps.

DTO validation.summary: DTO validation checks inbound shapes at the API boundary so invalid data never reaches domain logic.
DTO validation.problem: Trusting client JSON enables mass assignment and subtle invariant breaks.
DTO validation.mechanics: Define DTOs/schemas, reject unknown fields, validate types/ranges, and return structured errors.
DTO validation.tradeoffs: Strict validation improves safety but needs careful versioning when clients lag.
DTO validation.troubleshoot: If bad payloads succeed, ensure ValidationPipe whitelist+forbidNonWhitelisted is on.
DTO validation.example:
@IsString() @MinLength(1) name: string;
// ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true })
DTO validation.integration: 1) Add schema validation globally. 2) Forbid unknown props. 3) Share error format. 4) Contract-test samples.

dynamic module.summary: Nest dynamic modules configure providers at import time via forRoot/forRootAsync for reusable libraries.
dynamic module.problem: Hard-coded config in shared modules prevents reuse across environments.
dynamic module.mechanics: Expose register methods that accept config, provide tokens, and export services for importers.
dynamic module.tradeoffs: Dynamic modules are flexible but harder to follow—document tokens clearly.
dynamic module.troubleshoot: If config undefined, Async factory deps aren't imported—wire ConfigModule.
dynamic module.integration: 1) Convert shared libs to forRootAsync. 2) Inject config tokens. 3) Document. 4) Test module compile.

environment configuration.summary: Environment configuration injects 12-factor settings (DB URLs, secrets, feature flags) without baking them into images.
environment configuration.problem: Committed secrets and undocumented env vars cause breaches and 'works on my machine' failures.
environment configuration.mechanics: Load env via ConfigModule, validate with zod/joi at boot, fail fast on missing required vars.
environment configuration.tradeoffs: Many envs increase matrix complexity; prefer same artifact, different config.
environment configuration.troubleshoot: If boot succeeds with wrong DB, validation is incomplete—require critical keys.
environment configuration.integration: 1) Schema-validate env at boot. 2) Keep secrets in a vault. 3) Document vars. 4) Same image across envs.

ES modules.summary: ESM is Node's official module system with import/export, better static analysis, and asynchronous loading semantics.
ES modules.problem: Dual CJS/ESM packages cause 'ERR_REQUIRE_ESM' and duplicated instances of singleton libs.
ES modules.mechanics: Prefer ESM for new code, set package exports carefully, and avoid dual publishing pitfalls.
ES modules.tradeoffs: ESM is future-proof but some tooling/CJS deps still friction; use documented interop patterns.
ES modules.troubleshoot: If default import is undefined, check CJS interop and named export mismatch.
ES modules.integration: 1) Adopt ESM. 2) Fix exports map. 3) Resolve dual-package hazards. 4) Update loaders/tests.

execution context.summary: Nest ExecutionContext wraps the current request handler info so guards/interceptors can introspect class/handler/protocol.
execution context.problem: Auth logic that assumes HTTP fails for GraphQL/RPC or can't read metadata reflectors.
execution context.mechanics: Use context.switchToHttp().getRequest() for HTTP, read roles via Reflector, keep guards protocol-aware.
execution context.tradeoffs: Abstraction helps multi-transport apps; pure HTTP apps can keep it simple.
execution context.troubleshoot: If request is undefined, wrong switch method for transport.
execution context.example:
const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
const roles = this.reflector.get('roles', ctx.getHandler());
execution context.integration: 1) Centralize guards using ExecutionContext. 2) Use Reflector. 3) Test HTTP+any other transports.

graceful shutdown.summary: Graceful shutdown stops accepting new work, drains in-flight requests/jobs, then exits—critical for deploys/K8s.
graceful shutdown.problem: Hard kills mid-write cause partial transactions and connection resets for clients.
graceful shutdown.mechanics: Listen for SIGTERM, stop health readiness, close HTTP server with timeout, flush telemetry, then exit.
graceful shutdown.tradeoffs: Long drains delay rollouts; too short cuts requests—align with LB idle timeouts.
graceful shutdown.troubleshoot: If pods get SIGKILL, drain exceeds terminationGracePeriodSeconds—tune both.
graceful shutdown.integration: 1) Handle SIGTERM. 2) Fail readiness first. 3) Drain with timeout. 4) Align K8s grace. 5) Test rolling deploys.

guard.summary: Nest guards determine whether a route can run (authn/authz), running after middleware and before pipes/interceptors.
guard.problem: Auth checks duplicated in services are easy to miss on new endpoints.
guard.mechanics: Implement CanActivate, read metadata, validate credentials/permissions, and register globally or per-route.
guard.tradeoffs: Guards keep controllers clean; over-smart guards become mini-frameworks—keep focused.
guard.troubleshoot: If open routes exist, enforce global auth with explicit @Public() opt-outs.
guard.integration: 1) Global AuthGuard. 2) Role metadata. 3) @Public exceptions. 4) Integration tests per role.

hexagonal architecture.summary: Hexagonal (ports & adapters) isolates domain logic from delivery/persistence adapters via interfaces.
hexagonal architecture.problem: Domain code that imports Nest/ORM details becomes untestable outside the framework.
hexagonal architecture.mechanics: Define ports in domain, implement adapters for DB/HTTP, inject via DI at composition root.
hexagonal architecture.tradeoffs: Clear boundaries vs more indirection; apply where complexity justifies.
hexagonal architecture.troubleshoot: If tests need DB for domain rules, boundary leaked—introduce ports.
hexagonal architecture.example:
// domain/OrderService depends on OrderRepository port
// infra/PrismaOrderRepository implements port
hexagonal architecture.integration: 1) Identify domain core. 2) Define ports. 3) Move ORM to adapters. 4) Test domain pure. 5) Wire in Nest module.

HTTP semantics.summary: HTTP semantics define methods, status codes, headers, and idempotency expectations clients rely on.
HTTP semantics.problem: Misusing GET for mutations or 200 for creates breaks caches and client logic.
HTTP semantics.mechanics: Use method meaning correctly, pick precise statuses, document error bodies, and set cache headers deliberately.
HTTP semantics.tradeoffs: Pragmatic APIs sometimes bend REST purity—document deviations explicitly.
HTTP semantics.troubleshoot: If CDNs cache POSTs or miss GETs, review method safety and Cache-Control.
HTTP semantics.example:
POST /orders → 201 Created + Location
PUT /orders/{id} → idempotent replace
HTTP semantics.integration: 1) Document method semantics. 2) Standardize error envelope. 3) Add contract tests. 4) Review caching.

idempotency.summary: Idempotency ensures repeating the same logical request (retries) does not apply side effects twice.
idempotency.problem: Network retries on POST without keys double-charge payments and create duplicate rows.
idempotency.mechanics: Require keys on mutating POSTs, store response/status by key+actor, and replay on retries.
idempotency.tradeoffs: Storage cost vs safety; TTL keys carefully. PUT/DELETE are often naturally idempotent.
idempotency.troubleshoot: If duplicates appear, keys missing or uniqueness not enforced atomically.
idempotency.example:
UNIQUE(user_id, idempotency_key)
-- return stored response when key exists
idempotency.integration: 1) Add Idempotency-Key on payments. 2) Persist outcomes. 3) Atomic insert. 4) Client retry policy. 5) Metrics.

interceptor.summary: Nest interceptors wrap handler execution for cross-cutting concerns: logging, mapping, caching, timeouts.
interceptor.problem: Duplicated try/catch mapping in every controller drifts.
interceptor.mechanics: Implement NestInterceptor, use next.handle().pipe(...), and register globally when broadly useful.
interceptor.tradeoffs: Powerful but opaque if overused; prefer pipes for validation and filters for errors.
interceptor.troubleshoot: If response shape wrong, check interceptor order.
interceptor.integration: 1) Add logging/transform interceptors. 2) Keep them focused. 3) Document order. 4) Test.

job queue.summary: Job queues persist background work (emails, image processing) with retries, concurrency, and delayed jobs.
job queue.problem: Doing slow work in HTTP requests times out and couples UX to downstream failures.
job queue.mechanics: Enqueue from API after durable write, process in workers, retry with backoff, DLQ failures.
job queue.tradeoffs: Queues improve resilience but require ops (Redis/BullMQ). Sync may be fine for tiny tasks.
job queue.troubleshoot: If jobs stuck, check worker health, failed sets, and poison payloads.
job queue.example: await queue.add('email', { userId }, { attempts: 5, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 } });
job queue.integration: 1) Introduce queue. 2) Move slow tasks. 3) Idempotent workers. 4) DLQ alerts. 5) Dashboard lag.

JWT access token.summary: JWTs are signed bearer tokens carrying claims so APIs can authenticate without server session lookup each time.
JWT access token.problem: Long-lived JWTs in localStorage are hard to revoke and XSS-stealable; trusting unverified tokens is fatal.
JWT access token.mechanics: Issue short-lived access tokens, verify signature/exp/aud, authorize from claims, and store refresh tokens carefully (often httpOnly).
JWT access token.tradeoffs: Stateless scale vs revocation difficulty; use blocklists or short TTL+refresh rotation for logout.
JWT access token.troubleshoot: If forged tokens work, you skipped verify or used a weak secret; rotate keys and validate aud/iss.
JWT access token.example: const payload = await jose.jwtVerify(token, key, { issuer, audience });
JWT access token.integration: 1) Short TTL access tokens. 2) Verify all claims. 3) Secure refresh storage. 4) Rotate keys. 5) Prefer opaque tokens if revocation is critical.

keep-alive.summary: HTTP keep-alive reuses TCP connections for multiple requests, reducing handshake latency.
keep-alive.problem: Disabled keep-alive under load spikes latency/CPU on TLS handshakes.
keep-alive.mechanics: Enable keep-alive agents for outbound HTTP, tune idle timeouts vs LBs, and monitor connection churn.
keep-alive.tradeoffs: Too-long idle can hit middlebox timeouts; too-short loses benefits.
keep-alive.troubleshoot: If many SYN packets, agents aren't reusing—fix agent config.
keep-alive.example: const agent = new https.Agent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 64 });
keep-alive.integration: 1) Enable agents. 2) Align timeouts. 3) Load-test. 4) Monitor churn.

libuv thread pool.summary: libuv's threadpool (default 4) handles some Node fs/dns/crypto tasks off the JS thread.
libuv thread pool.problem: Saturating the pool makes fs-heavy apps appear 'blocked' even when the JS loop looks idle.
libuv thread pool.mechanics: Measure, increase threadpool judiciously, prefer async APIs, and move heavy CPU to dedicated workers.
libuv thread pool.tradeoffs: Bigger pools help until hardware saturates; not a fix for bad algorithms.
libuv thread pool.troubleshoot: If fs latency high with idle loop, pool may be saturated—profile.
libuv thread pool.integration: 1) Measure fs/crypto latency. 2) Tune pool. 3) Offload extreme CPU. 4) Document runtime env.

load balancing.summary: Load balancers distribute traffic across instances for scale and availability with health checks.
load balancing.problem: Uneven routing and failing health checks cause cascading overload on remaining nodes.
load balancing.mechanics: Place LB in front, health-check readiness, drain on deploy, and keep services as stateless as possible.
load balancing.tradeoffs: Sticky sessions ease stateful apps but hurt failover; prefer shared stores.
load balancing.troubleshoot: If one node hot, check sticky cookies and unbalanced least-conn settings.
load balancing.example: # readiness fails during drain; LB removes instance before SIGTERM completes
load balancing.integration: 1) Stateless services. 2) Readiness probes. 3) Connection drain. 4) Test failover. 5) Watch per-node RPS.

mass assignment.summary: Mass assignment occurs when clients set sensitive fields (role, balance) because APIs bind raw JSON into models.
mass assignment.problem: Without allowlists, attackers escalate privileges via extra JSON properties.
mass assignment.mechanics: Use DTOs with explicit fields, forbid unknowns, and map manually to domain updates.
mass assignment.tradeoffs: Strict DTOs add boilerplate but prevent an entire vulnerability class.
mass assignment.troubleshoot: Try posting role:admin; if accepted, fix whitelist immediately.
mass assignment.integration: 1) DTO allowlists. 2) Forbid extras. 3) Security tests. 4) Review ORM entity binding.

metrics.summary: Metrics are numeric time-series (counters/histograms/gauges) for RED/USE monitoring and alerting.
metrics.problem: Logs alone cannot efficiently compute p99 or error rates across fleets.
metrics.mechanics: Instrument request rate/errors/duration, keep label cardinality bounded, and alert on SLO burn.
metrics.tradeoffs: Too many labels explode TSDB cost; too few can't debug.
metrics.troubleshoot: If metrics missing, check exporter scrape configs and service discovery.
metrics.integration: 1) Add RED metrics. 2) Bound labels. 3) SLO alerts. 4) Dashboard golden signals.

middleware.summary: Middleware sits in the HTTP pipeline before routing finishes concerns like logging, CORS, and raw body parsing.
middleware.problem: Order mistakes break auth (parsing body after auth) or double-parse payloads.
middleware.mechanics: Register cross-cutting HTTP concerns early, call next, and prefer guards/pipes for Nest-specific logic.
middleware.tradeoffs: Middleware is flexible but less typed than Nest guards; use the right layer.
middleware.troubleshoot: If req.body empty, parser middleware missing or consumed earlier.
middleware.integration: 1) Map pipeline order. 2) Keep middleware thin. 3) Prefer guards for auth. 4) Test order-sensitive paths.

modular monolith.summary: A modular monolith is a single deployable with strong internal module boundaries—often the best step before microservices.
modular monolith.problem: Microservices too early multiply ops cost without real team/scale need.
modular monolith.mechanics: Enforce module public APIs, separate schemas if needed, and forbid deep imports via lint.
modular monolith.tradeoffs: One deploy is simple; still requires discipline or it becomes a monolith ball of mud.
modular monolith.troubleshoot: If modules circularly import, boundaries are wrong—revisit context map.
modular monolith.example: orders/ public API only; inventory/ cannot import orders/internal/*
modular monolith.integration: 1) Define modules. 2) Lint boundaries. 3) Separate tables ownership. 4) Extract service only with evidence.

module.summary: Nest modules group providers/controllers and control export/import visibility for DI encapsulation.
module.problem: Everything-in-AppModule recreates a global mess and circular DI pain.
module.mechanics: Create feature modules, export only public providers, import what you need, avoid circular imports.
module.tradeoffs: More modules clarify ownership but increase wiring; find a balance.
module.troubleshoot: If Nest can't resolve deps, check exports of the providing module.
module.integration: 1) Split feature modules. 2) Export minimally. 3) Fix cycles. 4) Document public providers.

multi-tenant SaaS.summary: Multi-tenant SaaS serves many customers with isolation via tenant_id, schemas, or separate databases.
multi-tenant SaaS.problem: Missing tenant filters leak data across customers—the worst class of bug.
multi-tenant SaaS.mechanics: Resolve tenant per request, enforce filters in data layer, test cross-tenant access attempts, and isolate noisy neighbors.
multi-tenant SaaS.tradeoffs: Shared DB is cheaper; separate DBs isolate better at higher cost.
multi-tenant SaaS.troubleshoot: pen-test with another tenant's IDs; must 404/403.
multi-tenant SaaS.integration: 1) Tenant context middleware. 2) Enforce in repo layer. 3) Automated cross-tenant tests. 4) Quotas. 5) Audit logs.

N+1 query problem.summary: N+1 happens when code runs one query plus one query per row instead of a batched join/IN query.
N+1 query problem.problem: ORMs make N+1 easy via lazy relations, melting databases under list endpoints.
N+1 query problem.mechanics: Log SQL counts, eager-load or batch IDs, and add tests that fail when query count regresses.
N+1 query problem.tradeoffs: Joins can over-fetch; dataloaders batch well for graphs. Pick based on shape.
N+1 query problem.troubleshoot: APM showing thousands of similar SELECTs is classic N+1—fix the loop.
N+1 query problem.example:
// Bad: for (const u of users) await postsByUser(u.id)
// Good: SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = ANY($1)
N+1 query problem.integration: 1) Enable query logging in tests. 2) Fix list endpoints. 3) Add query-count budgets. 4) Review ORM includes.

NestJS.summary: NestJS is a structured Node framework using modules, DI, controllers, and providers inspired by Angular patterns.
NestJS.problem: Unstructured Express apps become hard to test and navigate as teams grow.
NestJS.mechanics: Organize by module, inject dependencies via constructors, push logic to services, and keep controllers thin.
NestJS.tradeoffs: Structure helps large apps but can feel heavy for tiny scripts—don't over-module early.
NestJS.troubleshoot: If DI fails (undefined provider), check module exports/imports and provider scope.
NestJS.integration: 1) Scaffold Nest module per domain. 2) Wire DI. 3) Add ValidationPipe. 4) Test with TestingModule. 5) Document module boundaries.

Node streams.summary: Streams process data in chunks (Readable/Writable/Transform/Duplex) to bound memory for large I/O.
Node streams.problem: Buffering entire uploads/downloads in memory OOMs under concurrency.
Node streams.mechanics: Use stream.pipeline for error-safe piping, respect backpressure, and prefer streaming parsers for large payloads.
Node streams.tradeoffs: Streams are efficient but harder APIs; for small JSON, buffers are fine.
Node streams.troubleshoot: If memory grows, you likely buffered; ensure pipe and pause/resume work.
Node streams.example:
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';
await pipeline(fs.createReadStream(src), gzip, fs.createWriteStream(dst));
Node streams.integration: 1) Stream uploads to object storage. 2) Use pipeline. 3) Handle errors. 4) Load-test large files.

Node.js event loop.summary: Node's event loop multiplexes async I/O on a single JS thread, offloading some work to libuv's threadpool.
Node.js event loop.problem: Blocking the loop with sync CPU/fs calls stalls all requests.
Node.js event loop.mechanics: Keep handlers non-blocking, tune UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE for fs/dns/crypto, and monitor event-loop lag.
Node.js event loop.tradeoffs: Single-threaded simplicity vs CPU scaling limits—use clustering/workers for CPU.
Node.js event loop.troubleshoot: High lag with low CPU may be sync FS; profile with clinic/0x.
Node.js event loop.example:
setImmediate(() => console.log('check phase'));
await fs.promises.readFile(path); // non-blocking API
Node.js event loop.integration: 1) Ban sync FS in request path. 2) Monitor loop delay. 3) Offload CPU. 4) Tune threadpool if needed.

notification service.summary: Notification services fan out email/SMS/push with templates, preferences, and delivery receipts.
notification service.problem: Sending directly from many services duplicates logic and ignores user preferences/unsubscribes.
notification service.mechanics: Enqueue notification commands, render templates, respect prefs/unsub, and retry with provider webhooks.
notification service.tradeoffs: Central service adds latency/ops but prevents spam and inconsistency.
notification service.troubleshoot: If duplicates, idempotency keys missing on provider calls.
notification service.integration: 1) Centralize notifications. 2) Prefs/unsub. 3) Idempotent provider calls. 4) Webhook status. 5) Metrics per channel.

OAuth 2.0.summary: OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization so clients obtain access tokens without handling user passwords directly.
OAuth 2.0.problem: Wrong grant types (implicit for SPAs) and missing PKCE enable token theft.
OAuth 2.0.mechanics: Use auth code with PKCE for public clients, limit scopes, rotate refresh tokens, and validate tokens on APIs.
OAuth 2.0.tradeoffs: OAuth complexity vs building login yourself—prefer trusted IdPs. Don't invent crypto.
OAuth 2.0.troubleshoot: If redirect attacks succeed, check redirect URI allowlists and state/PKCE params.
OAuth 2.0.integration: 1) Pick IdP. 2) Auth code+PKCE. 3) Tight redirect URIs. 4) Scope minimally. 5) Secure refresh rotation.

object storage.summary: Object storage (S3-compatible) stores blobs by key with durability and cheap scale vs local disk.
object storage.problem: App servers storing files locally lose data on redeploy and don't scale horizontally.
object storage.mechanics: Upload via presigned URLs or server streams, store keys in DB, set lifecycle/encryption, and scan for malware if user content.
object storage.tradeoffs: Public buckets are dangerous; prefer private + presign. Egress costs can surprise.
object storage.troubleshoot: If 403 on get, check IAM and presign expiry.
object storage.example: const url = await s3.getSignedUrl('putObject', { Bucket, Key, Expires: 900 });
object storage.integration: 1) Private buckets. 2) Presigned upload. 3) Persist keys. 4) Lifecycle rules. 5) Virus scan if needed.

OpenAPI.summary: OpenAPI describes HTTP APIs machine-readably for docs, client SDKs, and contract tests.
OpenAPI.problem: Undocumented APIs drift and break consumers silently.
OpenAPI.mechanics: Maintain spec as source or generate from code, publish docs, and fail CI on breaking changes.
OpenAPI.tradeoffs: Spec-first vs code-first: choose based on consumer needs; keep them synced.
OpenAPI.troubleshoot: If clients diverge, diff OpenAPI in CI and version breaks.
OpenAPI.example:
openapi: 3.1.0
paths:
  /health:
    get:
      responses:
        '200': { description: OK }
OpenAPI.integration: 1) Introduce OpenAPI. 2) Generate docs/clients. 3) Validate requests. 4) Breaking-change CI gate.

optimistic locking.summary: Optimistic locking detects concurrent updates via version columns instead of holding long DB locks.
optimistic locking.problem: Lost updates occur when two readers write stale copies last-write-wins.
optimistic locking.mechanics: Include version in UPDATE ... WHERE version=old; increment; on 0 rows return conflict for client retry.
optimistic locking.tradeoffs: Better concurrency than pessimistic locks for low contention; high contention needs different design.
optimistic locking.troubleshoot: If silent overwrites happen, version not checked—fix SQL.
optimistic locking.example: UPDATE accounts SET bal=$1, version=version+1 WHERE id=$2 AND version=$3
optimistic locking.integration: 1) Add version columns. 2) Enforce in repo. 3) Return 409. 4) Client refresh/retry. 5) Test concurrent writers.

ORM.summary: ORMs map tables to objects/query builders to speed CRUD while abstracting SQL dialects.
ORM.problem: Hiding SQL entirely invites N+1, unpredictable queries, and weak indexes.
ORM.mechanics: Use ORM for CRUD, explain critical queries, drop to SQL for complex reporting, and own migrations.
ORM.tradeoffs: Productivity vs control; hybrid approaches (Prisma + SQL) are common.
ORM.troubleshoot: If slow endpoints appear, EXPLAIN ORM SQL and check includes/joins.
ORM.example: const users = await prisma.user.findMany({ include: { posts: true } });
ORM.integration: 1) Adopt ORM with migrations. 2) Log SQL in staging. 3) Index hot paths. 4) Allow raw SQL where needed.

pagination.summary: Pagination returns result windows via offset/limit or cursors/keyset for stable large lists.
pagination.problem: Huge unbounded lists time out and freeze UIs; offset deep pages get slow and inconsistent under inserts.
pagination.mechanics: Prefer keyset on indexed (created_at,id), return next cursor, and avoid counting every time if expensive.
pagination.tradeoffs: Offset is simple for admin UIs; cursors for feeds at scale.
pagination.troubleshoot: If duplicates/skips while scrolling, sort key unstable—add unique tiebreaker.
pagination.example: SELECT * FROM items WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20
pagination.integration: 1) Replace offset feeds with cursors. 2) Index sort keys. 3) Document cursor opacity. 4) Optional approx totals.

password hashing.summary: Password hashing stores one-way salted hashes (Argon2/bcrypt) so breaches don't reveal raw passwords.
password hashing.problem: Plaintext or fast hashes (MD5) make credential stuffing trivial after a leak.
password hashing.mechanics: Hash with Argon2id, tune memory/time, compare in constant time, and migrate legacy hashes on login.
password hashing.tradeoffs: Higher work factors harden security but increase CPU—balance with UX and DoS protections.
password hashing.troubleshoot: If login CPU spikes, attackers may be DoSing hashing—rate-limit and CAPTCHA.
password hashing.example: const hash = await argon2.hash(password, { type: argon2.argon2id });
password hashing.integration: 1) Argon2id. 2) Rate-limit auth. 3) Migrate old hashes. 4) Breach monitoring. 5) Forbid password logs.

payment API.summary: Payment APIs must be idempotent, PCI-aware (usually via providers), and explicit about capture/refund states.
payment API.problem: Retries without idempotency double-charge; storing raw card data creates compliance nightmares.
payment API.mechanics: Use a PSP, store tokens not PANs, idempotent create/capture, verify webhooks, and reconcile ledgers.
payment API.tradeoffs: Building your own card vault is almost never worth it—use Stripe-like providers.
payment API.troubleshoot: If money mismatches, reconcile provider events vs ledger by payment id.
payment API.example:
POST /v1/charges Idempotency-Key: ...
# webhook: payment_intent.succeeded → mark paid
payment API.integration: 1) Integrate PSP. 2) Idempotent charges. 3) Webhook verify. 4) Ledger entries. 5) Reconciliation job.

pipe.summary: Nest pipes transform and validate input (ValidationPipe, ParseUUIDPipe) before handlers run.
pipe.problem: Manual parsing in every handler duplicates and misses edge cases.
pipe.mechanics: Register ValidationPipe globally, use param pipes, and keep transformations explicit.
pipe.tradeoffs: Pipes are perfect for input; don't hide domain rules inside them.
pipe.troubleshoot: If validation skipped, pipe not global and route lacks DTO types.
pipe.example: app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));
pipe.integration: 1) Global ValidationPipe. 2) Param pipes. 3) Structured errors. 4) Tests for invalid payloads.

PostgreSQL full-text search.summary: Postgres FTS uses tsvector/tsquery and GIN indexes for linguistic search inside the database.
PostgreSQL full-text search.problem: ILIKE '%term%' cannot use normal B-tree indexes efficiently at scale.
PostgreSQL full-text search.mechanics: Maintain tsvector columns/triggers, GIN index them, query with to_tsquery, and rank with ts_rank.
PostgreSQL full-text search.tradeoffs: FTS is good enough for many apps; specialized search engines win for relevance/facets at larger scale.
PostgreSQL full-text search.troubleshoot: If searches sequential-scan, verify GIN and vector maintenance.
PostgreSQL full-text search.example:
CREATE INDEX ON articles USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', body));
SELECT * FROM articles WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', $1);
PostgreSQL full-text search.integration: 1) Add tsvector+GIN. 2) Rank results. 3) Measure. 4) Consider OpenSearch if relevance needs grow.

profiling.summary: Profiling samples CPU/heap to find hot functions and leaks instead of guessing.
profiling.problem: Optimizing without profiles wastes time on the wrong 90%.
profiling.mechanics: Capture under realistic load, open flamegraphs, fix top frames, and re-measure.
profiling.tradeoffs: Sampling overhead is usually small; still avoid leaving debug profilers always-on carelessly.
profiling.troubleshoot: If profiles empty, missing symbols/source maps—fix build flags.
profiling.integration: 1) Baseline latency. 2) Profile under load. 3) Fix top hotspots. 4) Automate periodic profiles in staging.

provider and dependency injection.summary: Nest providers are injectable classes/values registered in modules; DI wires constructor dependencies automatically.
provider and dependency injection.problem: Manual `new Service()` bypasses DI and makes testing/lifecycle hooks harder.
provider and dependency injection.mechanics: Annotate @Injectable, register providers, inject via constructor, override in tests with custom providers.
provider and dependency injection.tradeoffs: DI clarifies graphs but circular deps signal design smells.
provider and dependency injection.troubleshoot: If undefined dependency, provider missing from module providers/exports.
provider and dependency injection.integration: 1) Register providers. 2) Inject constructors. 3) Use tokens for interfaces. 4) Override in tests.

provider scopes.summary: Nest provider scopes (DEFAULT singleton, REQUEST, TRANSIENT) control instance lifetime.
provider scopes.problem: Request-scoped providers bubble and can surprise performance if overused.
provider scopes.mechanics: Keep most services singleton; use REQUEST for request-bound context sparingly; understand scope propagation.
provider scopes.tradeoffs: Request scope solves context passing but hurts throughput—prefer ALS for request ids when possible.
provider scopes.troubleshoot: If memory grows per request, a request-scoped tree is retaining too much.
provider scopes.integration: 1) Default singleton. 2) Limit REQUEST scope. 3) Measure. 4) Prefer ALS for simple context.

RabbitMQ.summary: RabbitMQ is a message broker implementing AMQP with exchanges, queues, bindings, and ack semantics for async work.
RabbitMQ.problem: Sync chains between services create fragility; unacked consumers redeliver forever without poison handling.
RabbitMQ.mechanics: Publish to exchanges, consume with manual ack after success, set prefetch, and route failures to DLQ.
RabbitMQ.tradeoffs: Brokers decouple producers/consumers but add ops burden; managed queues trade control for simplicity.
RabbitMQ.troubleshoot: If messages pile up, check consumer errors, prefetch, and routing keys.
RabbitMQ.integration: 1) Define topology. 2) Idempotent consumers. 3) DLQ+alerts. 4) Load-test prefetch. 5) Document schemas.

race condition.summary: Race conditions occur when concurrent operations interleave unsafely on shared state, yielding lost updates or duplicates.
race condition.problem: Check-then-act without transactions/constraints fails under concurrency.
race condition.mechanics: Enforce invariants in DB constraints/transactions, avoid TOCTOU, and test with parallel requests.
race condition.tradeoffs: App-level locks are fragile vs DB constraints; prefer DB as source of truth.
race condition.troubleshoot: Reproduce with parallel k6/ab; if fails, add constraint/transaction.
race condition.integration: 1) Identify shared invariants. 2) Enforce in DB. 3) Concurrent tests. 4) Remove check-then-act.

rate limiting.summary: Rate limiting caps request rates per key (IP/user/API key) to protect availability and control abuse.
rate limiting.problem: Unauthenticated expensive endpoints get DoSed or scraped.
rate limiting.mechanics: Apply limits at edge/API gateway and app, return 429 with headers, and store counters in Redis for multi-node.
rate limiting.tradeoffs: Strict limits protect systems but can block NAT users sharing IPs—prefer user keys when authenticated.
rate limiting.troubleshoot: If limit not enforced across nodes, local memory store—move to Redis.
rate limiting.integration: 1) Identify expensive routes. 2) Redis-backed limits. 3) 429 headers. 4) Tune with product. 5) Monitor.

RBAC.summary: Role-based access control grants permissions via roles assigned to subjects rather than per-user ACLs alone.
RBAC.problem: Hard-coded role checks scattered in controllers drift and miss edge routes.
RBAC.mechanics: Centralize permission maps, enforce in guards, and combine with resource ownership checks for multi-tenant data.
RBAC.tradeoffs: RBAC is simple until roles explode; ABAC/ReBAC may fit complex domains.
RBAC.troubleshoot: If unauthorized access works, add integration tests per role and audit default-deny.
RBAC.integration: 1) Define permission matrix. 2) Enforce in guards. 3) Default deny. 4) Audit logs. 5) Test each role.

Redis TTL.summary: Redis TTL expires keys automatically—used for sessions, locks, and cache entries that must not live forever.
Redis TTL.problem: Keys without TTL grow memory forever; locks without TTL deadlock holders that crash.
Redis TTL.mechanics: Set TTL on write (SET key val EX seconds), renew deliberately for sessions, and monitor evictions.
Redis TTL.tradeoffs: Short TTL reduces staleness/memory but increases misses; sliding sessions need careful refresh.
Redis TTL.troubleshoot: If memory high, find keys without TTL (SCAN) and add expires or eviction policy.
Redis TTL.example:
SET session:123 '{...}' EX 3600
SET lock:order:9 token NX EX 30
Redis TTL.integration: 1) Default TTL on cache keys. 2) TTL all locks. 3) Alert memory. 4) Document key prefixes.

resource ownership checks.summary: Ownership checks ensure the authenticated principal can act only on resources they own (or are shared with).
resource ownership checks.problem: AuthN without ownership checks lets users access /orders/{someoneElsesId}.
resource ownership checks.mechanics: Load resource, compare owner/tenant to principal, deny consistently, and test IDOR attempts.
resource ownership checks.tradeoffs: 404 obscures existence; 403 is clearer—pick a policy and stick to it.
resource ownership checks.troubleshoot: IDOR test: authenticate as A, access B's id—must fail.
resource ownership checks.integration: 1) Centralize ownership helper. 2) Use on all by-id routes. 3) IDOR tests. 4) Audit logs.

response serialization.summary: Response serialization maps domain entities to public DTOs, hiding internal fields and shaping API contracts.
response serialization.problem: Returning ORM entities leaks password hashes and internal columns.
response serialization.mechanics: Use interceptor/serializer to expose allowlisted fields; never return raw entities.
response serialization.tradeoffs: Manual mapping is clear; automated exclude decorators can be forgotten—review carefully.
response serialization.troubleshoot: If hash leaks, entity was returned—add serialization tests.
response serialization.integration: 1) Response DTOs. 2) Global serializer. 3) Leak tests. 4) Document public fields.

REST resource design.summary: REST resource design models nouns as resources with HTTP methods acting on representations and hypermedia/relations as needed.
REST resource design.problem: RPC-ish endpoints (/doThing) proliferate and confuse caching/idempotency.
REST resource design.mechanics: Name resources consistently, use plural collections, nest carefully, and document error shapes.
REST resource design.tradeoffs: Pure REST vs pragmatic RPC: choose clarity for clients; consistency beats dogma.
REST resource design.troubleshoot: If clients misuse methods, your docs/examples are unclear—tighten contract tests.
REST resource design.integration: 1) Agree naming conventions. 2) Map verbs to methods. 3) Add OpenAPI. 4) Review nesting depth.

retry and dead-letter queue.summary: Retries re-attempt failed jobs with backoff; DLQs hold poison messages after exhaustion for human/automated review.
retry and dead-letter queue.problem: Infinite retries without DLQ hot-loop CPU and block queues.
retry and dead-letter queue.mechanics: Configure attempts/backoff, ack only on success, route to DLQ, and page on DLQ growth.
retry and dead-letter queue.tradeoffs: Retries help transient faults; non-idempotent handlers make retries dangerous.
retry and dead-letter queue.troubleshoot: If DLQ fills, inspect payloads and fix consumer bugs before redrive.
retry and dead-letter queue.example: attempts: 5, backoff: exponential, removeOnFail: false // inspect failed set / DLQ
retry and dead-letter queue.integration: 1) Idempotent consumers. 2) Backoff retries. 3) DLQ. 4) Alerts. 5) Redrive runbook.

retry with backoff.summary: Retry with backoff spaces attempts (often exponential + jitter) to let transient faults recover without stampedes.
retry with backoff.problem: Immediate tight retries amplify outages and trip rate limits.
retry with backoff.mechanics: Retry only transient errors, add jittered delay, cap attempts, and bubble final failure.
retry with backoff.tradeoffs: Backoff helps clients and servers; don't retry non-idempotent POSTs without keys.
retry with backoff.troubleshoot: If you still stampede, missing jitter—add randomized delay.
retry with backoff.example: await retry(() => fetch(url), { retries: 5, factor: 2, minTimeout: 100, jitter: true });
retry with backoff.integration: 1) Classify transient errors. 2) Library with jitter. 3) Idempotency. 4) Metrics on retry counts.

saga.summary: Sagas coordinate multi-step business processes across services with compensating actions when a step fails.
saga.problem: Distributed transactions (2PC) are rarely practical; partial failures leave inconsistent states.
saga.mechanics: Model steps/compensations, persist saga state, and ensure each step can retry safely.
saga.tradeoffs: Sagas add complexity; sometimes a modular monolith transaction is better.
saga.troubleshoot: If stuck mid-saga, inspect state store and compensation failures.
saga.example: // orchestrator: ReserveStock → ChargeCard → CreateShipment; compensations reverse
saga.integration: 1) Decide choreography/orchestration. 2) Persist state. 3) Compensations. 4) Timeouts. 5) Dashboards.

secrets management.summary: Secrets management stores credentials in a vault/manager with rotation and audited access—not in git or images.
secrets management.problem: Leaked .env in repos and baked Docker secrets cause breaches.
secrets management.mechanics: Inject secrets at runtime, rotate regularly, scope IAM tightly, and scan git history for leaks.
secrets management.tradeoffs: Vault ops cost vs cloud secret managers convenience—pick what you'll actually operate.
secrets management.troubleshoot: If secret leaked, rotate immediately and review access logs.
secrets management.example: # AWS SM / GCP Secret Manager / Vault KV; never COPY .env into Docker images
secrets management.integration: 1) Move secrets to manager. 2) Remove from git. 3) Rotate. 4) IAM least privilege. 5) Pre-commit secret scan.

service boundary.summary: Service boundaries define ownership of data and behavior so teams can deploy independently with clear contracts.
service boundary.problem: Random network splits without data ownership create distributed monoliths.
service boundary.mechanics: Split by domain ownership, prohibit cross-service DB access, and communicate via APIs/events.
service boundary.tradeoffs: More services increase isolation and ops cost; start coarse.
service boundary.troubleshoot: If you need joins across services constantly, boundary is wrong.
service boundary.example: // orders service owns orders tables; inventory exposes ReserveStock API/events
service boundary.integration: 1) Map ownership. 2) Kill shared DB access. 3) Publish contracts. 4) Review sync coupling.

session authentication.summary: Session authentication stores server-side session state referenced by an opaque cookie id.
session authentication.problem: Client-side-only auth without revocation options complicates logout and theft response.
session authentication.mechanics: Create session on login, set HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie, validate server-side, destroy on logout.
session authentication.tradeoffs: Easy revocation vs sticky store scaling; Redis sessions are common.
session authentication.troubleshoot: If sessions persist after logout, destroy server record and expire cookie.
session authentication.example:
req.session.userId = user.id;
// cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
session authentication.integration: 1) Server sessions. 2) Secure cookies. 3) CSRF defenses. 4) Redis store. 5) Rotate session ids.

SSE.summary: Server-Sent Events stream one-way text events over HTTP from server to browser—simple live updates.
SSE.problem: Polling wastes load; full WebSockets are heavier when only server→client is needed.
SSE.mechanics: Send event-stream responses, write named events, include ids for resume, and disable proxy buffering.
SSE.tradeoffs: SSE is simple but unidirectional and has connection limits per browser; WS needed for bidirectional chat.
SSE.troubleshoot: If events delay, check nginx buffering and compression settings.
SSE.integration: 1) Pick SSE for one-way feeds. 2) Add event ids. 3) Configure proxies. 4) Heartbeat comments. 5) Auth the stream.

SSRF.summary: Server-side request forgery tricks your server into requesting internal URLs (metadata, admin panels) on an attacker's behalf.
SSRF.problem: URL-fetch features without allowlists expose cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) and intranet services.
SSRF.mechanics: Validate URLs, resolve DNS and deny private ranges, restrict protocols, and prefer allowlists over denylists.
SSRF.tradeoffs: Allowlists are safer but less flexible for user webhooks—use egress proxies with policy.
SSRF.troubleshoot: Test with internal IPs; if reachable, fix validation and IMDS hop limits.
SSRF.example: // Reject private/link-local after DNS resolve before fetch
SSRF.integration: 1) Inventory URL fetchers. 2) Allowlist. 3) Block private CIDRs. 4) Lock down cloud metadata. 5) Add security tests.

stateless API.summary: Stateless APIs keep authorization/state in the request (token/headers) so any instance can serve it.
stateless API.problem: In-memory session affinity complicates horizontal scale and failover.
stateless API.mechanics: Externalize session/cache state, verify auth each request, and design handlers without local process memory requirements.
stateless API.tradeoffs: Truly stateless simplifies scale; some state (WS) still needs sticky or shared pubsub.
stateless API.troubleshoot: If only one node works for a user, you have sticky state—externalize it.
stateless API.example: // JWT or session id backed by Redis — any node can validate
stateless API.integration: 1) Externalize state. 2) Auth each request. 3) Remove sticky needs. 4) Test multi-instance locally.

streamed upload.summary: Streamed uploads pipe request bodies directly to storage without buffering entire files in memory.
streamed upload.problem: Buffering multi-GB uploads crashes Node under concurrency.
streamed upload.mechanics: Use streaming multipart middleware, pipe to S3, enforce size limits, and process scans asynchronously.
streamed upload.tradeoffs: Streaming is efficient; error handling mid-stream needs cleanup of partial objects.
streamed upload.troubleshoot: If RSS spikes on upload, buffering remains—switch to true streaming APIs.
streamed upload.example: await pipeline(req, fs.createWriteStream(tmp)); // or s3.upload({ Body: req })
streamed upload.integration: 1) Stream to object storage. 2) Size caps. 3) Cleanup partials. 4) Async malware scan. 5) Load-test.

structured logging.summary: Structured logging emits JSON fields (level, msg, requestId, userId) for queryable observability.
structured logging.problem: String-only logs are hard to filter and correlate during incidents.
structured logging.mechanics: Use pino/winston JSON, include requestIds, redact secrets/PII, and ship to a log backend.
structured logging.tradeoffs: Debug logs in prod explode cost; sample or raise levels carefully.
structured logging.troubleshoot: If you can't filter by user, fields missing—standardize schema.
structured logging.integration: 1) JSON logger. 2) Field standard. 3) Redaction. 4) Ship to stack. 5) Dashboards/alerts.

timeout.summary: Timeouts bound how long you wait on dependencies so failures surface instead of hanging forever.
timeout.problem: No timeouts exhaust connection pools as requests pile up waiting on dead deps.
timeout.mechanics: Set explicit timeouts on HTTP/DB calls, cancel work when possible, and map to 504/503 appropriately.
timeout.tradeoffs: Too aggressive timeouts false-fail; too long hold resources—align with SLOs.
timeout.troubleshoot: If pools exhaust, hung calls without timeouts—add them and circuit breakers.
timeout.integration: 1) Default client timeouts. 2) Propagate deadlines. 3) Align with LB. 4) Alert on timeout rates.

transaction boundary.summary: Transaction boundaries group DB operations that must commit or roll back together to preserve invariants.
transaction boundary.problem: Multi-step writes without transactions leave partial state on mid-failure.
transaction boundary.mechanics: Open transaction, perform related writes, commit; never call payment providers inside holding DB locks.
transaction boundary.tradeoffs: Wide transactions increase contention; chatty small transactions can break invariants—balance carefully.
transaction boundary.troubleshoot: If partial rows remain after errors, missing transaction or catch swallowed rollback.
transaction boundary.integration: 1) Identify invariants. 2) Wrap in transactions. 3) Keep short. 4) Outbox for external side effects. 5) Tests for mid-fail.

unit test.summary: Unit tests verify pure logic and services with dependencies mocked/faked for fast feedback.
unit test.problem: No unit tests make refactors scary; over-mocking tests implementation not behavior.
unit test.mechanics: Test domain rules with fakes, avoid mocking everything, and keep tests readable.
unit test.tradeoffs: Unit speed vs integration confidence—use both deliberately.
unit test.troubleshoot: If tests break on renames only, you over-mocked—assert behavior.
unit test.integration: 1) Unit-test domain. 2) Mock IO boundaries. 3) Fast CI target. 4) Pair with API integration tests.

URL shortener.summary: URL shorteners map compact codes to destination URLs with redirects, analytics, and abuse controls.
URL shortener.problem: Predictable IDs enable scraping; missing HTTPS/open-redirect checks enable phishing.
URL shortener.mechanics: Generate unguessable codes, store mapping, redirect safely after validation, and monitor for malware URLs.
URL shortener.tradeoffs: Short TTLs vs permanent links; analytics storage can dominate cost.
URL shortener.troubleshoot: If collisions occur, increase code space and check uniqueness constraints.
URL shortener.example:
INSERT INTO links(code,url) VALUES($1,$2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
// GET /:code → 302 Location: url
URL shortener.integration: 1) Design code space. 2) Validate destinations. 3) Rate-limit creates. 4) Abuse scanning. 5) Cache redirects.

WebSocket.summary: WebSockets provide full-duplex channels over a long-lived TCP connection after an HTTP upgrade.
WebSocket.problem: Using request/response for high-frequency bidirectional chat adds latency and load.
WebSocket.mechanics: Authenticate on connect, heartbeat, handle reconnect, and fanout via Redis/NATS when multiple nodes.
WebSocket.tradeoffs: Stateful connections complicate load balancing; SSE/polling may suffice for simpler cases.
WebSocket.troubleshoot: If intermittent drops, check idle timeouts/proxies and ping intervals.
WebSocket.integration: 1) Auth connect. 2) Heartbeats. 3) Pub/sub for multi-instance. 4) Backpressure limits. 5) Reconnect protocol.

worker threads.summary: worker_threads run JS in parallel threads sharing memory optionally via SharedArrayBuffer/MessageChannel.
worker threads.problem: CPU-heavy work on the main thread blocks all request handling.
worker threads.mechanics: Offload CPU tasks to a worker pool, pass data via postMessage, and return results to the request path carefully.
worker threads.tradeoffs: Threads help CPU; IO-bound work usually doesn't need them. Pool sizing matters.
worker threads.troubleshoot: If still blocked, work isn't offloaded or pool is size 1 under load.
worker threads.example:
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';
const result = await runInWorker(payload);
worker threads.integration: 1) Identify CPU hotspots. 2) Worker pool. 3) Benchmark. 4) Fallback timeout. 5) Monitor pool queue.
